claims.text: Standard casting or solidification of HfNbTaTiZr produces a somewhat inhomogeneous microstructure with potential nascent phase separation.
Thermal-expansion-mismatch-induced internal stresses govern the alloy's unusual stress–strain behavior.
Thermal-expansion-mismatch-induced internal stresses govern the alloy's thermoelastic behavior.
Internal stresses generated during cooling drive the nucleation of nano-precipitates.
Internal stresses generated during cooling drive the growth of nano-precipitates.
Nano-precipitates and associated residual stresses modify the alloy's mechanical properties over a wide temperature range.
Rapid cooling from high processing temperatures promotes thermal-expansion mismatch relative to slow cooling or homogenization.
Slow cooling or homogenization minimizes mismatch-induced stresses.
Differential thermal contraction of constituent phases produces local phase segregation or nano-precipitates and residual stress fields.
Different thermal expansion coefficients within the alloy generate mismatch stresses during rapid cooling.
Mismatch stresses nucleate nano-precipitates during rapid cooling.
The nano-precipitates impede dislocation motion and thereby raise hardness.
Localized internal stresses associated with the precipitates alter the elastic moduli.
The precipitates may provide preferential paths for high-temperature creep.
Rapidly cooled samples will have higher microhardness than slowly cooled or homogenized samples.
Rapidly cooled samples will exhibit different temperature-dependent elastic moduli from slowly cooled or homogenized samples between 293 K and 1100 K.
Rapidly cooled samples will exhibit increased creep rates at 1250 °C relative to slowly cooled or homogenized samples.
Slow cooling or post-solidification homogenization results in a more uniform microstructure with fewer precipitate-induced effects.
The proposed mechanism is most applicable when rapid cooling from solidification temperatures produces significant thermal-expansion mismatch.
At temperatures significantly above 1250 °C or well below room temperature, mechanisms other than the proposed mismatch mechanism may dominate.
